snippet.title: In the 19th Century, Going to the Doctor Could Kill You | Nat Geo Explores
snippet.description:
The American medical profession was largely unregulated and dangerous prior to the discovery of the germ in the 19th century. However, the discovery of germs revolutionized medicine, transforming it into the prestigious practice and field of study that we know today.

snippet.title: Dark Medical History: Experiments, Lobotomy & Medical Horrors
snippet.description:
Explore the dark history of medicine in this comprehensive 3 hour Documentary designed for sleep and learning. From ancient trepanation to lobotomy, thalidomide disasters to radium poisoning, discover how medical mistakes shaped modern healthcare. This bedtime history documentary covers bloodletting, the Radium Girls tragedy, dangerous pharmaceuticals like cocaine and heroin, and psychiatric treatments that went terribly wrong.

02:39:15 Insulin Shock Therapy - Coma for Treatment

This sleep-friendly documentary combines rigorous historical research with calm, soothing narration perfect for falling asleep or deep learning. Unlike typical history content, our approach maintains a steady, unhurried pace that helps you relax while absorbing fascinating stories about medical history's darkest chapters. Each story is presented with respect for those affected, focusing on the lessons learned and the reforms that followed these tragedies.

SleepHistorian creates long-form history documentaries designed for sleep, relaxation, and deep learning. Every video combines thorough research with calm narration, helping you fall asleep while exploring fascinating historical topics. We upload new 2+ hour documentaries every Tuesday and Friday, covering everything from ancient civilizations to modern history's most intriguing stories.

This documentary on medical history's dark chapters examines how treatments like bloodletting, lobotomy, and dangerous pharmaceuticals persisted despite causing harm. We explore the thalidomide tragedy that changed drug testing forever, the Radium Girls whose lawsuit established workplace safety laws, and Frances Kelsey's determination that saved America from disaster. From ancient trepanation to insulin shock therapy, each story reveals how medical mistakes led to the patient protections and ethical standards we have today. This bedtime history documentary provides both education and relaxation, perfect for anyone interested in medical history, the history of science, or simply wanting calm, intelligent content for sleep.

Whether you're interested in the history of medicine, pharmaceutical disasters, psychiatric treatment evolution, or how modern medical ethics developed, this comprehensive documentary covers the key moments when medicine went wrong and the reforms that followed. The calm narration and steady pacing make it ideal for falling asleep, while the thoroughly researched content ensures you're learning accurate, meaningful history.

snippet.title: The Deadliest Infectious Disease of All Time | Crash Course Lecture
snippet.description:
Tuberculosis is often thought of as an old-timey disease, but in reality, it continues to kill over a million and a half people per year, despite its known cure. If you’ve been following author and TB-hater John Green in any way for the last year or so, this video is the deep dive you’ve been waiting for…

snippet.title: Curious Medical Habits From the Past | History for Sleep
snippet.description:
Throughout history, medical understanding has evolved alongside observation, tradition, and experimentation. Practices that once seemed logical or necessary were often shaped by the knowledge and beliefs available at the time.

This educational historical documentary explores a range of curious medical habits from the past. Drawing on medical texts, physicians’ notes, personal accounts, and modern historical research, the video gently examines how people approached health, illness, and care in earlier periods.

Rather than focusing on dramatic or unsettling details, the narrative reflects on context and intention: how treatments were developed, how communities understood the body, and how medical practices gradually changed as knowledge advanced.

Through calm storytelling and careful historical context, the video offers a thoughtful look at the history of medicine — revealing how human attempts to understand and care for the body have evolved over time.

This video is created for educational purposes in a calm, sleep-friendly format.
It is designed to inform gently and provide a peaceful listening experience.

#HistoryForSleep #MedicalHistory #HistoryOfMedicine #SocialHistory #DailyLifeHistory #WeirdHistory #HealthHistory

snippet.title: Dark Origins of Big Pharma: John D. Rockefeller’s Empire | Forgotten History Shorts
snippet.description:
Modern medicine as we know it wasn’t shaped by doctors alone—it was engineered by John D. Rockefeller. In the early 20th century, Rockefeller and his oil empire helped transform medicine into a pharmaceutical industry, sidelining natural remedies and alternative medicine in favor of synthetic, patented drugs.

🚨 Was this a revolution in healthcare or a calculated power move?
💰 Did Rockefeller create Big Pharma for profit, not public health?

🔎 In this episode of Forgotten History, we uncover the hidden story of how Rockefeller took control of medicine, the rise of Big Pharma, and why natural treatments were pushed aside in favor of prescription drugs. snippet.title: What did people do before anesthesia? - Sally Frampton
snippet.description:
Trace the history of anesthesia from the 3rd century to today, and explore how doctors performed surgery before anesthetic drugs.

--

The quest for anesthetics that could induce unconsciousness and enable more meticulous surgeries began around the early 3rd century CE. Before anesthesia was widely used, patients had to consciously endure every moment of surgery. So, what methods did doctors use before modern medicine caught up? Sally Frampton traces the history of anesthetic drugs.

snippet.title: The True Terrors Of Tudor Medicine | Hidden Killers | Timeline
snippet.description:
Dr Suzannah Lipscomb takes us back to Tudor times in search of the household killers of the era.

It was a great age of exploration and science where adventurers returned from the New World with exotic goods previously unknown in Europe. An era in which the newly emergent middle classes had, for the first time, money for luxuries and early consumer goods, many of which contained hidden dangers.

The period also saw a radical evolution in the very idea of 'home'. For the likes of Tudor merchants, their houses became multi-room structures instead of the single-room habitations that had been the norm (aristocracy excepted). This forced the homebuilders of the day to engineer radical new design solutions and technologies, some of which were lethal.

Suzannah discovers that in Tudor houses the threat of a grisly, unpleasant death was never far away in a world (and a home) still mired in the grime and filth of the medieval period - and she shows how we still live with the legacy of some of these killers today.

snippet.title: History of Medicine - Long, Relaxing Sleepy Story/Documentary
snippet.description:
This bedtime story video is about medicine and healing since the Neolithic. I will tell you about Ancient Mesopotamia and the first diagnoses and prescriptions, Ancient Egypt and the figure of Imhotep, India, and the principles of Ayurveda, or Chinese Medicine including Moxibustion and Acupuncture. We will also take a look at medicine in Ancient Greece and Rome, including important figures like Hippocrates and Galen, and how this legacy passed on and was further developed in the Islamic World, Byzantium, and Medieval Europe. Then we reach the Renaissance and the steps that would lead to an increasingly scientific approach to medicine and the many discoveries of the 19th and 20th centuries, that came with important social change and professionalization (I tell you at the end about scientists like Pasteur or Koch, and Florence Nightingale, the founder of modern nursing).

snippet.title: Uncover The Truth Behind "Patient Zero" (AIDS)
snippet.description:
The story of the AIDS epidemic and the man accused of starting it.
When a new, deadly virus spreads across North America at an alarming rate, one man is singled out for bringing the disease to the continent.

Spanning the 1970s until today, the story of Gaetan Dugas –aka ‘Patient Zero’ –serves as the perfect microcosm of the evolution of AIDS in America and the country’s response to it.

In the early 1980s, little was known about this global epidemic, except that it seemed to be most prevalent amongst gay men. America was in the grip of fear and uncertainty and, in the scramble for answers, Dugas would become known and vilified as ‘Patient Zero’.

Exploring timely themes about fear, the demonizing of the unknown, and the danger of false narratives, this FadooProductions and Fine Point Films documentary weaves social history and scientific investigation into a poignant story of an individual who became intrinsically and tragically linked with AIDS.

snippet.title: How Dangerous Really Was Medieval Healthcare?
snippet.description:
In the medieval world, the line between a miracle cure and a death sentence was razor-thin. We often dismiss the Middle Ages as a time of medical ignorance, but the foundations of modern healthcare were laid in the wards of medieval hospitals like The Commandery. In this documentary, join historian Matt Lewis as we step inside the world of the barber surgeon and the physician to uncover the truth about the four humors. From the strange practice of tasting urine to diagnose diabetes, to the "life-saving" application of blood-sucking leeches and cauterizing irons, we explore the brutal yet surprisingly logical reality of 14th-century medicine. We also investigate how the medieval world grappled with the terrifying arrival of Leprosy and the Black Death, revealing that many of our modern concepts of quarantine and hygiene are centuries older than we think.

Uncover the turbulent history of Bethlem Royal Hospital—infamously known as “Bedlam”—the world’s first institution dedicated to treating mental illness. This video traces its origins in 13th‑century London, revealing how shifting medical theories, religious attitudes, and social pressures shaped early psychiatric care. Explore the hospital’s notorious reputation for overcrowding, public “madhouse” tours, and controversial treatments, while meeting the reformers who fought to replace cruelty with compassion and science.

By examining archival records, patient stories, and recent scholarship, we reveal how Bethlem evolved from a medieval priory into a modern psychiatric institution, laying the groundwork for mental‑health practices worldwide. Whether you’re researching the roots of psychology, London’s hidden history, or the broader struggle for humane treatment, this deep dive into Bethlem Royal Hospital offers essential insight into the challenges and breakthroughs that continue to influence mental‑health care today.

snippet.description:
How DANGEROUS was the medicine of the past? In this medical history documentary from History Calling we look at some of the most famous medical treatments employed by our ancestors that we would now consider to be at best useless and at worst nothing short of murder or attempted murder by killer doctors. As we explore the history of medicine, you’ll find out what trepanning was and why you don’t ever want to be subjected to it. We’ll look at how the English tried to battle the Great Plague of 1665 with masks and herbs. You’ll hear how the practice of bleeding nearly wiped out the French royal succession and what killed President George Washington, why Elizabeth I was lucky to survive smallpox given the bizarre treatment she was subjected to, the poisons like mercury administered for centuries as though they were medicines (plus whether Abraham Lincoln had mercury poisoning), the attempts to combine religion with medicine that involved supposedly magic rings and dead bodies, the recipe for a healing ointment invented by Henry VIII, the bonkers idea that smoking was somehow beneficial and so many more. I’ll also show you some medical instruments from the past used for these murderous medical treatments, including drills for the skull and lancets for drawing blood. Stay til the end of the video and I’ll even share with you one medieval medical treatment that actually worked and saved the life of a future King of England. By the end of the video you’ll understand why doctors were dangerous in the past, including as recently as the 20th century in some cases and why the sick and injured might have been better off going it alone back in the day.

snippet.title: Britain's Abandoned Asylums: Where Medicine Became Suffering | Complete Dark History Documentary
snippet.description:
Walking through abandoned hospital corridors decades after closure, the institutional green paint still peels in long strips. Each layer represents a decade of promises that psychiatric care would finally work. The promises consistently failed.

Tonight, we journey through six of Britain's most notorious abandoned asylums. Real places you can visit. Real suffering documented in hospital records. Real people whose stories reveal what society tried to forget.

From Bedlam, where visitors paid to watch patients as entertainment, to Severalls Hospital, where experimental procedures permanently altered thousands of brains. From Whittingham, where systematic abuse led to national scandal, to Cane Hill, which ended consumed by flames.

These are not ghost stories. These are documented histories of places where medicine caused lasting harm, where architectural beauty could not overcome institutional cruelty, where the promise of healing masked decades of confinement.

snippet.title: One of the most controversial medical procedures in history - Jenell Johnson
snippet.description:
Uncover the history of the lobotomy, and find out why it's considered one of the most controversial procedures of the 20th century.

--

In 1935, researchers found that after removing the frontal lobes of two chimps, they no longer experienced frustration or anxiety. Neurologist Egas Moniz believed that replicating this in humans could cure mental illness— leading to one of the most controversial and destructive medical treatments of the 20th century: the lobotomy. Jenell Johnson uncovers the history of the procedure.

Lesson by Jenell Johnson, directed by Anton Bogaty.

snippet.description:
Support our human made, non AI content! Join from £3 on Patreon or YT Memberships for extra videos & bonus content, funded and influenced directly by you! https://www.patreon.com/cw/OfficialMedievalMadness

The disease known as the plague has been stalking humanity for over 5,000 years, and there have been many outbreaks. In fact, there have been three pandemics caused by the bacillus bacterium Yersinia Pestis. The first was in the 6th century. It devastated the Byzantine Empire and was known as The Plague of Justinian. The third began in China in the mid-19th century and quickly spread throughout the world. But it is the plague that began in 1346 which killed more than 50 million people in just seven years that we refer to as the ‘Black Death’. The Middle Ages was a time of superstition, religious fanaticism and ignorance and so they thought it was the end of the world. In reality it was the largest pandemic in the history of humanity.
